claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 exhibits significant porosity and microstructural defects.
Porosity and microstructural defects in conventionally sintered ZrB2 cause premature failure during liquid plating-bath exposure.
SPS at 2100–2200 °C and 50–100 MPa can consolidate single-phase ZrB2 at a lower temperature than conventional sintering.
Rapid heating, short dwell times, and applied pressure during SPS will reduce porosity in ZrB2.
In-situ high-temperature imaging such as X-ray tomography can monitor and optimize densification and pore evolution during ZrB2 sintering.
The SPS intervention will enhance particle-neck formation and grain-boundary diffusion.
Enhanced neck formation and grain-boundary diffusion will produce a denser and more homogeneous ZrB2 microstructure with fewer pores.
Transient high current and applied pressure in SPS promote rapid mass transport in ZrB2.
Rapid mass transport accelerates neck formation between ZrB2 particles.
Shortened consolidation time reduces the opportunity for pore coarsening and minimizes microstructural defects.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will achieve full densification at approximately 2100–2200 °C.
Compared with ZrB2 conventionally sintered above 2300 °C, SPS-processed ZrB2 will have lower porosity, higher density, and better mechanical integrity.
Reduced porosity and enhanced mechanical integrity will improve resistance to degradation during prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath.
The proposed preparation boundary is 2100–2300 °C under controlled pressure conditions.
The proposed service boundary is exposure to liquid plating baths maintained at 50–100 °C.
Effects outside the specified preparation and service ranges remain untested.
The magnitude of porosity reduction and mechanical-property improvement under long-term plating conditions is uncertain.
The scalability of in-situ imaging for routine process optimization remains un demonstrated.
